title: Multiple Interface Bounds
story: Your data processing pipeline needs items that can be cloned AND compared AND displayed. One constraint isn't enough — you need all three. Multiple interface bounds express complex requirements cleanly.
why: Multiple interface bounds (T: A + B + C) express complex type requirements precisely, ensuring functions only accept types with all needed capabilities.
analogy: A job posting requires: 'Must have a degree AND 3 years experience AND a driver's license.' All three are mandatory — meeting just two won't get you hired. Multiple interface bounds are the same: the type must satisfy ALL constraints, not just some.
try_it: Add a third interface `Timestamped` with `fn created_at(&self) -> Int`. Make Record implement it. Update `archive` to require all three interfaces. Create a second type that implements only two and try passing it to archive — observe the compiler error.
tips: Use `+` between interface names: `T: A + B + C`
The compiler checks ALL bounds — if any are missing, it won't compile
Order doesn't matter: `T: A + B` is the same as `T: B + A`
common_mistakes: Using commas instead of +: `T: A, B` is wrong — use `T: A + B`
Implementing only some of the required interfaces — must implement ALL
Adding unnecessary bounds — only require what the function actually uses
